questions.question: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A class is a reference type; a struct is a value type. I choose based on semantics first: an Order has identity and is normally a class, while a small immutable Money or Coordinate can be a struct.
questions.detailedAnswer: The key differences are copying, identity, nullability, inheritance rules and boxing. Large or mutable structs can be expensive and confusing because assignments copy the value. Structs are strongest for small value-like data.

questions.seniorPerspective: A senior answer connects the language rule to domain semantics and performance evidence rather than saying structs are always faster.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a struct only because it is a value type; creating large mutable structs; ignoring boxing and copying.

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and abstract class in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: An interface defines a contract that unrelated types can implement; an abstract class can provide shared state and implementation. I prefer interfaces for replaceable dependencies and abstract classes only when there is real shared behavior.
questions.detailedAnswer: Interfaces support multiple implementations and keep dependencies loosely coupled. Abstract classes are useful when common implementation is part of the design, but they create stronger inheritance coupling.
questions.example: A transaction service can depend on an IPaymentGateway interface. The production implementation talks to the bank, while a test can inject a fake gateway. I would use an abstract class only when several implementations genuinely share workflow and state.
questions.seniorPerspective: The important senior decision is whether the abstraction represents a capability or a shared implementation.
questions.commonMistakes: Creating interfaces for every class without a meaningful boundary; using inheritance just to reuse a few lines of code.

questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable represents iteration over data already available to the application, while IQueryable can build an expression that a provider such as EF Core translates into a database query.

questions.question: What are async and await used for in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: They let an application start an asynchronous operation and continue without blocking a thread while I/O is pending. They improve scalability for I/O-bound work; they do not automatically make CPU work faster.
questions.detailedAnswer: Async is most valuable for I/O such as HTTP, database, files and messaging. CPU-heavy work needs a different strategy; wrapping synchronous CPU work in Task.Run inside a server request is not a universal performance fix.
questions.example: If an ATM backend calls a database or another service, the request thread does not need to sit blocked while I/O is running. Using async/await lets the application handle other work while it waits, then continue when the operation completes.
questions.seniorPerspective: I look for end-to-end async flow and avoid blocking with Result or Wait, especially in server code.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling .Result or .Wait; using async void for normal application code; assuming async means parallel.

questions.question: What are Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes in ASP.NET Core dependency injection?
questions.shortAnswer: Transient creates a new instance each time requested, Scoped normally creates one per request scope, and Singleton keeps one instance for the application lifetime.
questions.detailedAnswer: The lifetime must match state ownership and thread-safety. A singleton must not capture a scoped dependency, and mutable singleton state needs synchronization or should be avoided.
questions.example: An ATM transaction service needs logging, configuration and a database client. Instead of creating each dependency inside the service, the constructor receives them. That makes the service easier to test and lets production configuration decide which implementation is used.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose a lifetime by ownership and concurrency semantics, not by habit.
questions.commonMistakes: Registering everything as singleton; injecting scoped services into singletons; storing request-specific state in singleton objects.

questions.question: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Middleware is a component in the HTTP request pipeline that can inspect, modify, short-circuit or pass a request to the next component.
questions.detailedAnswer: Ordering matters because middleware wraps later components. Authentication must run before authorization, and short-circuiting middleware can prevent the endpoint from executing.
questions.example: For an ATM API, request logging can run early, authentication must run before protected endpoints, and exception handling should be positioned so it can catch downstream failures. Middleware order therefore affects the actual request behavior.
questions.seniorPerspective: I explain middleware as an ordered pipeline and discuss why the order changes behavior.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating middleware order as cosmetic; putting endpoint-specific logic into global middleware; exposing exception details to clients.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Dependency injection supplies a class's dependencies from outside instead of making the class construct them itself. It reduces coupling and improves testing and replacement.
questions.detailedAnswer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit. DI also centralizes lifecycle management and allows infrastructure implementations to change without rewriting business logic.
questions.example: An ATM transaction service needs logging, configuration and a database client. Instead of creating each dependency inside the service, the constructor receives them. That makes the service easier to test and lets production configuration decide which implementation is used.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior value is not the container itself; it is dependency direction and clear boundaries.
questions.commonMistakes: Injecting dozens of services into one class; hiding required dependencies in service locators; creating infrastructure objects directly inside business logic.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its lexical scope even after the outer function has returned.
questions.detailedAnswer: Closures are useful for encapsulation and callbacks, but long-lived closures can retain references and contribute to memory leaks if attached to long-lived objects or subscriptions.

questions.question: What is the difference between let, const and var?
questions.shortAnswer: let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped. const prevents reassignment of the binding but does not make an object immutable.

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.shortAnswer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and adds matching right-side data when available.
questions.detailedAnswer: Join choice is driven by the business result set. A LEFT JOIN followed by a WHERE condition on the right table can accidentally behave like an INNER JOIN.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I verify the expected row cardinality with a small dataset before tuning the query.
questions.commonMistakes: Choosing joins by habit; filtering the right table in WHERE unintentionally; ignoring duplicate rows caused by one-to-many relationships.
followUps: How would you find customers with no orders?

questions.question: What is an index and why does it improve query performance?
questions.shortAnswer: An index is an additional data structure that helps the database locate rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds some reads but adds storage and write cost.
questions.detailedAnswer: Indexes should follow actual predicates, joins and ordering patterns. Too many indexes increase insert and update cost and can still be ineffective when selectivity is poor.

questions.question: What is a transaction?
questions.shortAnswer: A transaction groups related database changes so the database can enforce an atomic unit of work according to the chosen isolation level.
questions.detailedAnswer: Transactions protect consistency, but long transactions increase locking and contention. The correct boundary should be as small as possible while protecting the required invariant.
questions.example: If the transaction history screen is slow, I would first inspect the query plan and execution time. If users frequently search by AccountId and TransactionDate, a suitable index can reduce the rows SQL Server needs to scan, but I would verify the write and storage cost too.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define the business invariant first, then choose the smallest transaction that guarantees it.
questions.commonMistakes: Opening transactions around slow external calls; assuming transactions solve distributed consistency; ignoring isolation and lock duration.

questions.shortAnswer: I start with clients, API boundaries, business logic, data stores, external dependencies, asynchronous messaging where needed, observability and security.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that authenticated identity is allowed to do.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication answers identity; authorization answers permission. Authorization must be enforced server-side for protected resources.

questions.question: What is RAG and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant approved information and supplies it to the model before generation, reducing dependence on model memory for changing or private knowledge.
questions.detailedAnswer: A production RAG pipeline needs chunking, metadata, retrieval quality, prompt construction, access control and evaluation; retrieval alone does not guarantee a correct answer.

questions.question: What is the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks sequentially?
questions.shortAnswer: Task.WhenAll allows independent asynchronous operations to progress concurrently; sequential awaits wait for one operation before starting the next if the tasks are created sequentially.
questions.detailedAnswer: Concurrency is appropriate only when operations are independent and downstream capacity can handle it. It does not make one database query inherently faster.

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ and why can it surprise developers?
questions.shortAnswer: Many LINQ operators build a query that executes when enumerated rather than when defined. This means the source can change or expensive work can run multiple times.
questions.detailedAnswer: Materialize deliberately when you need a stable snapshot or when repeated enumeration would be expensive. Keep provider-backed queries controlled so database work is explicit.
questions.example: Suppose I need the successful ATM transactions from the last hour. I can express the filter with LINQ, but with EF Core I also need to check whether the query is translated to SQL efficiently instead of loading thousands of rows into memory first.
questions.seniorPerspective: I watch execution boundaries and do not assume a LINQ variable contains data merely because the query expression was created.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling Count then ToList and accidentally executing two queries; enumerating expensive sequences repeatedly; hiding database calls behind properties.
followUps: When does ToList execute?

questions.question: How does exception handling affect API design?
questions.shortAnswer: Exceptions should represent unexpected or exceptional failures, while expected business outcomes can be modeled explicitly. API middleware should translate unhandled exceptions into consistent responses without leaking internals.
questions.detailedAnswer: A good design separates logging, client response mapping and domain behavior. Exceptions should retain diagnostic context while responses expose only appropriate information.

questions.seniorPerspective: I want one consistent error contract, structured logs and clear ownership of where errors are handled.
questions.commonMistakes: Catching Exception everywhere; returning stack traces to clients; logging the same exception at every layer; using exceptions for normal control flow.

questions.question: How would you prevent an N+1 query problem in EF Core?

questions.question: What is the difference between value types and reference types in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Value types hold their value directly; reference types hold a reference to an object. Assigning a value type copies the value, while assigning a reference type copies the reference.
questions.detailedAnswer: This affects mutation, parameter passing, nullability and memory behavior. Boxing can move a value type into an object representation.
questions.example: A transaction amount can be a value-like decimal, while an Account object has identity and can be shared by several parts of the application.
questions.seniorPerspective: At senior level I explain the semantic reason for the choice, then consider copying cost, mutability and allocation rather than memorizing stack-versus-heap rules.

questions.question: What is boxing and unboxing in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Boxing converts a value type to object or an implemented interface; unboxing extracts the value type again. Boxing can allocate and should not happen accidentally in hot paths.
questions.detailedAnswer: Generic collections usually avoid unnecessary boxing because the type is known at compile time. Boxing can still occur through object, non-generic APIs or interface use.
questions.example: If an ATM transaction processor stores every numeric value in object, repeated boxing can create avoidable allocations.
questions.seniorPerspective: I look for boxing in performance-sensitive code using profiling rather than assuming every conversion is expensive.
questions.commonMistakes: Casting unrelated types; using object-based APIs unnecessarily; overlooking allocation in tight loops.
questions.codeExample: Box = value into object; unbox = object back to value.

questions.question: What is the difference between ref, out and in parameters?
questions.shortAnswer: ref passes an existing variable by reference, out requires the method to assign a value, and in passes a readonly reference to an existing value.
questions.detailedAnswer: They express different API contracts. out is useful for multiple return values in some APIs, ref permits mutation, and in can avoid copying larger readonly structs.
questions.example: A parser may use out for a parsed value and success flag, while a performance-sensitive method may use in for a large readonly value type.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use these features only when they make the contract clearer or solve a measured allocation/copying concern.
questions.commonMistakes: Using ref when a return value would be clearer; forgetting that in still requires a valid argument.
questions.followUps: Can ref return values be used?

questions.question: What are records in C# and when would you use them?
questions.shortAnswer: Records are designed for data-centric models with value-based equality and concise immutable-style syntax. They are useful for DTOs and messages where identity is based on data.
questions.detailedAnswer: record class and record struct provide different reference/value semantics. The with expression creates a modified copy without mutating the original record.
questions.example: An ATM API response DTO can be a record because two responses with the same fields can be considered equivalent for many tests.
questions.seniorPerspective: I avoid using records for domain entities whose identity and lifecycle matter independently of their field values.
questions.commonMistakes: Using records for mutable tracked entities without understanding equality; assuming records are automatically deeply immutable.

questions.question: What is the difference between string and StringBuilder?
questions.shortAnswer: string is immutable, so repeated concatenation can create multiple string objects. StringBuilder is useful when many modifications are performed in a loop.
questions.detailedAnswer: For a few concatenations, normal string interpolation is clearer. StringBuilder becomes useful when constructing large text incrementally.
questions.example: Generating a large ATM audit report line by line can benefit from StringBuilder rather than repeatedly creating intermediate strings.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on workload and profiling, not because StringBuilder is always faster.
questions.commonMistakes: Using StringBuilder for tiny expressions; forgetting to call ToString; assuming interpolation is always slow.

questions.question: What is covariance and contravariance in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Variance lets compatible generic interfaces and delegates convert between related types in safe directions. Covariance uses out and contravariance uses in.
questions.detailedAnswer: IEnumerable<out T> is a common covariant example because a sequence of a derived type can be read as a sequence of its base type.
questions.example: A reporting service can expose IEnumerable<ATMTransaction> where consumers only need IEnumerable<Transaction> if the relationship is valid.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior concern is substitutability: variance should preserve type safety and communicate whether a generic abstraction produces or consumes values.
questions.commonMistakes: Expecting classes to be variant; trying to mutate a covariant collection through a base type.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: The .NET GC reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable. It uses generations to optimize collection based on object lifetime.
questions.detailedAnswer: GC does not eliminate all memory problems. Long-lived references, event handlers, caches and unmanaged resources can keep objects alive or leak outside managed memory.
questions.example: If an ATM monitoring service keeps every historical transaction in a static list, the objects remain reachable and memory grows even though GC is working correctly.
questions.seniorPerspective: I inspect allocation rate, GC pauses, object retention and process memory before changing code or GC settings.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying GC frees every object immediately; confusing managed memory leaks with native resource leaks.

questions.question: What is IDisposable and why is using important?
questions.shortAnswer: IDisposable gives a deterministic way to release resources such as streams, database connections and handles. using ensures Dispose is called even when an exception occurs.
questions.detailedAnswer: Managed objects are collected by GC, but external resources have their own lifetime. async using is the corresponding pattern for IAsyncDisposable.
questions.example: A database connection should be disposed after the operation so pooled resources return promptly to the pool.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior engineers make ownership explicit: the code that creates or owns a disposable resource should define how it is released.
questions.commonMistakes: Relying on GC to close connections; disposing an object that another component owns; missing async disposal for async resources.

questions.question: What is the difference between an ASP.NET Core controller and minimal API endpoint?
questions.shortAnswer: Controllers provide a structured MVC-style programming model, while minimal APIs offer a lightweight endpoint style with less ceremony.
questions.detailedAnswer: Both can use dependency injection, middleware, validation and authorization. The choice is mainly about API structure, conventions and team needs.
questions.example: A small health endpoint can be minimal; a large enterprise API with many resource controllers may benefit from controller conventions.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose the style that keeps endpoint contracts, filters, validation and testing understandable at the application's scale.

questions.question: What is model binding in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Model binding maps HTTP route, query, form or body data into action parameters or request models.
questions.detailedAnswer: It reduces manual parsing but should be combined with validation. Binding success does not automatically mean the business input is valid.
questions.example: A transaction endpoint can bind accountId from the route and amount from the JSON body, then validate both before processing.
questions.seniorPerspective: I keep transport models separate from domain models when the API boundary needs different validation or security rules.

questions.question: What is the difference between IActionResult, ActionResult<T> and IResult?
questions.shortAnswer: They are different ways to express HTTP endpoint results. ActionResult<T> is useful in controller APIs when a successful result has a known body type but errors can also be returned.
questions.detailedAnswer: IResult is common with minimal APIs. The important point is keeping the HTTP contract explicit rather than returning arbitrary objects.
questions.example: A withdrawal endpoint may return a TransactionDto on success and a meaningful ProblemDetails response on failure.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define success and failure contracts intentionally so Angular or other clients can handle them predictably.

questions.question: What is ProblemDetails in ASP.NET Core?

questions.question: What is configuration and the Options pattern in ASP.NET Core?

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in ASP.NET Core?

questions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: Declarations are processed before execution in their scope, but let and const remain inaccessible in the temporal dead zone until initialized. Function declarations are also hoisted.
questions.detailedAnswer: Hoisting is about how declarations are handled, not that every variable can be safely used before its declaration.
questions.example: A function declaration can be called before its source position, but a const variable cannot be accessed before initialization.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: == allows type coercion while === compares without implicit type conversion. In application code I normally prefer === because the comparison contract is explicit.
questions.detailedAnswer: Loose equality has defined coercion rules, but those rules can surprise readers. Strict equality reduces accidental matches.
questions.example: An API field that may be numeric or string should be normalized explicitly rather than relying on == to make values match.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior code makes data normalization explicit at boundaries.
questions.commonMistakes: Using == without understanding coercion; assuming === performs deep object comparison.

questions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the outer object but nested objects remain shared. A deep copy creates independent nested data.
questions.detailedAnswer: Object spread and Object.assign are shallow. structuredClone can deep-clone many structured values, but not every object type or behavior.
questions.example: If an Angular form state contains nested account details, a shallow copy can accidentally mutate the original nested object.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose copying based on the data model and immutability requirements rather than blindly cloning everything.

questions.question: What is event delegation in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: Event delegation attaches one handler to a common ancestor and uses event bubbling to handle events from matching descendants.

questions.example: A transaction table can use one click handler on the table instead of one listener per row.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use delegation when it simplifies dynamic DOM behavior, while Angular applications normally prefer component event binding.
questions.commonMistakes: Ignoring stopPropagation; relying on fragile DOM selectors; using raw DOM manipulation unnecessarily in Angular.

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
questions.shortAnswer: Both can describe shapes, but interfaces are especially useful for object contracts and declaration merging, while type aliases can express unions, intersections and other type compositions.
questions.detailedAnswer: The choice is often stylistic unless a specific feature matters. Both provide compile-time typing and disappear at runtime.
questions.example: An API response can be an interface, while a status field can be a union type such as 'Pending' | 'Completed'.
questions.seniorPerspective: I optimize for readable domain contracts rather than enforcing a universal interface-versus-type rule.

questions.question: How does the JavaScript event loop handle asynchronous work?
questions.shortAnswer: JavaScript runs synchronous code on the call stack and schedules asynchronous callbacks through queues that are processed when the stack is clear.
questions.detailedAnswer: Microtasks such as promise continuations are processed before the next task in the browser event loop. This ordering explains many timing surprises.
questions.example: An Angular API response callback does not interrupt currently running JavaScript; it is scheduled and handled after the current work completes.

questions.question: What is normalization in relational databases?
questions.shortAnswer: Normalization organizes data to reduce unnecessary duplication and update anomalies by separating related facts into appropriate tables.
questions.detailedAnswer: The goal is data correctness and maintainability. Highly normalized schemas can sometimes require more joins, so read-heavy designs may intentionally denormalize with evidence.
questions.example: Customer details should not be copied into every ATM transaction row if a stable customer key can reference one customer record.
questions.seniorPerspective: I start with a normalized model and denormalize only for a measured access pattern or reporting requirement.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating normalization as an absolute performance rule; creating tables so fragmented that normal operations become unnecessarily complex.

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
questions.shortAnswer: DELETE removes selected rows and can be filtered; TRUNCATE removes all rows with a more structural operation; DROP removes the table object itself.
questions.detailedAnswer: Transaction behavior, logging, identity handling, permissions and foreign-key constraints differ by operation and database engine.
questions.example: Deleting test transactions may use DELETE with a WHERE clause; clearing a disposable staging table may use TRUNCATE when appropriate.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on intent and operational safety, never using destructive commands casually in production.
questions.commonMistakes: Running DELETE without WHERE; assuming TRUNCATE is just faster DELETE; dropping objects when only data should be removed.

questions.question: What is a clustered index versus a nonclustered index?
questions.shortAnswer: A clustered index determines the physical/logical organization of table rows around its key in SQL Server, while a nonclustered index is a separate structure that points to the underlying rows.
questions.detailedAnswer: A table has one clustered index at most, while multiple nonclustered indexes can support different access patterns. Indexes improve reads but add write and storage cost.
questions.example: A transaction table might cluster on an appropriate key and add a nonclustered index for frequent searches by terminal ID and transaction time.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design indexes from actual query predicates, joins and ordering, then validate with execution plans and write impact.
questions.commonMistakes: Indexing every column; ignoring key order; assuming an index guarantees a fast query.
questions.followUps: How does a covering index work?

questions.question: What is a CTE and when would you use it?
questions.shortAnswer: A common table expression gives a named query expression that can improve readability and support recursive queries. It is not automatically a materialized temporary table.
questions.detailedAnswer: CTEs are useful for breaking complex queries into logical steps, but performance still depends on the resulting execution plan.
questions.example: A reporting query can first define eligible terminals in a CTE and then join transaction totals to that set.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use CTEs to make complex SQL understandable and inspect the plan rather than assuming the CTE itself improves performance.
questions.commonMistakes: Using CTEs as a performance guarantee; building huge nested CTE chains that obscure the query.

questions.question: What is a stored procedure and when would you use one?
questions.shortAnswer: A stored procedure packages database-side logic behind a callable interface. It can be useful for complex database operations, controlled access and established database-centric workflows.
questions.detailedAnswer: Stored procedures are not automatically faster than application code. Their value depends on data locality, operational ownership, security and maintainability.

questions.question: What is a window function in SQL?
questions.shortAnswer: A window function calculates a value across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group.
questions.detailedAnswer: Functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK and SUM OVER are useful for ranking, running totals and latest-record selection.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling versus vertical scaling?
questions.shortAnswer: Vertical scaling gives a machine more resources; horizontal scaling adds more instances. Horizontal scaling can improve capacity and resilience but requires distributed-state considerations.
questions.detailedAnswer: A stateless API is easier to scale horizontally because requests can be routed to different instances.
questions.example: An ATM service can run multiple API instances behind a load balancer while shared state lives in appropriate external systems.

questions.question: What is a load balancer and why is it used?
questions.shortAnswer: A load balancer distributes requests across healthy service instances and can remove unhealthy instances from rotation.
questions.detailedAnswer: It improves capacity and availability, but session affinity, connection handling, health checks and deployment behavior need consideration.
questions.example: Multiple ATM API instances can sit behind a load balancer so one instance failure does not stop all traffic.

questions.question: What is a message queue and when would you use one?
questions.shortAnswer: A message queue decouples producers from consumers so work can be processed asynchronously and retried according to defined policies.
questions.detailedAnswer: Queues help absorb bursts and isolate failures, but they introduce delivery semantics, ordering and eventual consistency.

questions.question: What is eventual consistency?

questions.question: What is idempotency and why is it important in distributed systems?
questions.shortAnswer: An idempotent operation can be repeated without producing additional unintended effects. It is important because clients and infrastructure may retry requests.
questions.detailedAnswer: The server can use an idempotency key and persist the result or operation state so a repeated request is recognized.
questions.example: For a cash withdrawal command, a retry must not create a second debit simply because the client did not receive the first response.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design idempotency around a stable business operation key and define how long the key/result is retained.

questions.question: What is the principle of least privilege?
questions.shortAnswer: Each identity or service should receive only the permissions required for its job and no more.
questions.detailedAnswer: Least privilege limits blast radius if credentials or components are compromised. It applies to users, APIs, database accounts, service identities and AI tools.

questions.question: What is a cache stampede and how can you prevent it?

questions.detailedAnswer: Mitigations include request coalescing, jittered TTLs, background refresh and stale-while-revalidate depending on correctness needs.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Encapsulation hides state behind controlled members, abstraction exposes only what callers need, inheritance reuses and specialises behaviour, and polymorphism lets the same contract produce different implementations.
questions.example: In an ATM application, a Transaction service can depend on an ITransactionProcessor interface while CashWithdrawalProcessor and CashDepositProcessor provide different behaviour.
questions.detailedAnswer: OOP is not just definitions: use encapsulation for invariants, abstraction for boundaries, inheritance only for a genuine is-a relationship, and polymorphism to avoid type-specific branching.
questions.seniorPerspective: I prefer composition and interfaces when behaviour varies independently; inheritance is useful when the subtype truly satisfies the base contract.
questions.commonMistakes: Confusing abstraction with encapsulation; using inheritance only to reuse code; violating substitutability.
followUps: What is composition?

questions.memoryCue: Four pillars = hide, simplify, specialise, substitute.

questions.question: What is encapsulation in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Encapsulation means keeping an object's state controlled and exposing operations that preserve its invariants.
questions.example: An ATM withdrawal object should not let callers directly set the available balance to an invalid value.
questions.detailedAnswer: Good encapsulation makes invalid states harder to create. Private fields, properties with controlled setters, and methods that enforce rules are common techniques.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use encapsulation to keep business rules close to the data they protect rather than scattering validation across controllers.
questions.commonMistakes: Making every property public with a setter; treating private fields as the only definition of encapsulation.
followUps: How would you make an object immutable?

questions.question: What is abstraction in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Abstraction exposes a useful contract while hiding implementation details.
questions.example: A payment service can expose ProcessPayment without exposing how the provider API, retries, and logging work.
questions.detailedAnswer: Interfaces and abstract classes are common abstraction mechanisms. The important point is the boundary, not simply hiding code.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior design uses abstractions where they reduce coupling and make substitution or testing useful, not for every single class.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying abstraction and encapsulation are identical; creating interfaces with no real boundary.
followUps: Interface vs abstract class?
questions.codeExample: public interface IPaymentService { Task ProcessPaymentAsync(decimal amount); }

questions.question: What is polymorphism in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Polymorphism allows code to work against a common contract while the concrete implementation determines behaviour.
questions.example: An ATM transaction handler can call Process on an ITransaction without knowing whether it is a withdrawal or deposit.
questions.detailedAnswer: Runtime polymorphism commonly uses virtual/override or interfaces. Compile-time polymorphism commonly refers to method overloading.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use polymorphism to remove large switch statements based on transaction type and make adding a new type safer.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling method overloading runtime polymorphism; using inheritance when composition would be clearer.
followUps: virtual vs override?

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
questions.shortAnswer: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameter signatures and is resolved at compile time. Overriding replaces virtual base behaviour and is resolved at runtime.
questions.example: A service may overload GetTransaction for different parameter sets, while a specialised processor overrides a virtual validation method.
questions.detailedAnswer: Overloading is about API convenience within a type. Overriding is about substitutable implementations in an inheritance hierarchy.
questions.seniorPerspective: I avoid overload sets that become ambiguous and use override only when the base contract genuinely permits custom behaviour.
questions.commonMistakes: Confusing overload resolution with virtual dispatch; changing only the return type does not create an overload.
followUps: What are new and sealed?
questions.memoryCue: Overload = different inputs; override = different implementation.
questions.codeExample: class A { public virtual string Get() => "A"; } class B : A { public override string Get() => "B"; }

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
questions.shortAnswer: An abstract class can share state and implementation with derived classes, while an interface defines a contract that unrelated classes can implement.
questions.example: A base ATM processor may share audit logic, while ITransactionHandler can be implemented by different handlers.
questions.detailedAnswer: Choose an abstract class when there is meaningful shared implementation and identity. Choose an interface for capability or a replaceable boundary.
questions.seniorPerspective: Modern C# interfaces can contain default implementations, so the practical distinction is about ownership, state, inheritance and design intent.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying interfaces can never contain implementation; using an abstract base class just to share unrelated utilities.
followUps: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
Can it inherit multiple classes?
questions.memoryCue: Abstract class = shared base; interface = capability/contract.
questions.codeExample: public interface IAuditable { void Audit(); } public abstract class TransactionBase { public abstract void Process(); }

questions.question: What is the difference between virtual, override, new and sealed?
questions.shortAnswer: virtual permits overriding, override supplies the derived implementation, new hides a base member, and sealed can prevent further overriding.
questions.example: A transaction base class can expose virtual validation that a specialised transaction overrides.
questions.detailedAnswer: new does not participate in normal virtual dispatch and can surprise callers when the object is referenced through the base type.
questions.seniorPerspective: I treat new method hiding as a deliberate compatibility choice and prefer override when polymorphism is intended.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming new is equivalent to override.
followUps: What happens when a sealed override is used?
questions.memoryCue: virtual opens; override replaces; new hides; sealed closes.

questions.question: What is a delegate in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. It lets code pass behaviour as a value.
questions.example: A transaction service can accept a delegate for a validation rule or callback.
questions.detailedAnswer: Delegates power callbacks, events, lambdas and APIs such as List<T>.Find. Func, Action and Predicate are common built-in delegate types.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use delegates when behaviour is supplied to an operation rather than when I need an independently managed event stream.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating a delegate as a raw function pointer without type safety; using delegates where a domain interface is clearer.
followUps: Delegate vs interface?

questions.question: What is the difference between Action, Func and Predicate?
questions.shortAnswer: Action represents a method returning void, Func represents a method returning a value, and Predicate is a delegate returning bool with one input.
questions.example: An ATM validation pipeline can use Predicate<Transaction> for a rule and Func<Transaction,Result> for transformation.
questions.detailedAnswer: The generic type parameters describe inputs and, for Func, the final parameter is the return type.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose the built-in delegate that communicates intent rather than declaring a custom delegate unnecessarily.
questions.commonMistakes: Mixing up Func's final generic argument as an input; using Predicate for multi-parameter APIs.
followUps: Can Func have multiple parameters?

questions.memoryCue: Action = no result; Func = result; Predicate = bool.

questions.question: What is an event in C# and how is it different from a delegate?
questions.shortAnswer: An event is a controlled publish-subscribe mechanism built on delegates. Subscribers can add or remove handlers, but outside code cannot normally raise the event.
questions.example: A transaction processor can raise TransactionCompleted when an ATM transaction finishes.
questions.detailedAnswer: The event keyword protects the publisher from external invocation. This makes ownership of raising the notification explicit.
questions.seniorPerspective: Events are useful when the publisher owns the lifecycle and consumers react independently.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating an event as a general-purpose callback parameter; forgetting to unsubscribe long-lived subscriptions.
followUps: Can events cause memory leaks?

questions.question: What are lambda expressions in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A lambda is a concise way to represent a function, commonly converted to a delegate or expression tree.
questions.example: Filtering transactions with transactions.Where(t => t.Amount > 1000) is a lambda-based predicate.
questions.detailedAnswer: Lambdas can capture variables, which creates closures, and in LINQ providers they may become expression trees rather than executable delegates.
questions.seniorPerspective: I watch for captured mutable state and whether a LINQ provider can translate the expression.
questions.commonMistakes: Ignoring closure capture; assuming every lambda executes immediately.

questions.question: What is a closure in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A closure occurs when a lambda or local function captures variables from its surrounding scope.
questions.example: A retry callback might capture a request identifier for logging.
questions.detailedAnswer: Captured variables can outlive the stack frame where they were declared. This matters for loops, asynchronous code and allocations.
questions.seniorPerspective: I inspect captured state when debugging surprising values or allocations in callbacks.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming a loop variable is copied independently in every closure; capturing mutable shared state.

questions.question: What are generics in C# and why are they useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Generics allow types and methods to work with a type parameter while preserving compile-time type safety and avoiding unnecessary casts.
questions.example: A repository can expose Repository<Transaction> instead of accepting object.
questions.detailedAnswer: Generics improve reuse without giving up type information. Constraints can restrict T to capabilities the implementation requires.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use generics for reusable infrastructure, collections and algorithms while keeping domain types explicit.
questions.commonMistakes: Using object everywhere instead of generics; adding overly complex generic abstractions.

questions.question: What are generic constraints in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Constraints restrict which types can be used as generic arguments and let the compiler guarantee required capabilities.
questions.example: A factory can require T : ITransaction so it can safely call transaction methods.
questions.detailedAnswer: Common constraints include class, struct, new(), base classes and interfaces.
questions.seniorPerspective: Constraints are useful when a generic algorithm genuinely needs a capability; they should not be added just to make a type hierarchy look sophisticated.
questions.commonMistakes: Using new() when dependency injection is actually needed; over-constraining reusable code.
followUps: What does where T : class mean?

questions.question: What is the difference between List, Dictionary, HashSet and Queue?
questions.shortAnswer: List is ordered indexed storage, Dictionary maps keys to values, HashSet stores unique values, and Queue provides FIFO processing.
questions.example: ATM pending requests can use a Queue, unique terminal IDs a HashSet, and terminal-to-status lookup a Dictionary.
questions.detailedAnswer: Choosing a collection depends on access pattern: lookup, uniqueness, ordering or FIFO processing.
questions.seniorPerspective: I start with required operations and complexity rather than choosing List by default.
questions.commonMistakes: Using List for repeated key lookups; using Dictionary when duplicate values are the real requirement.

questions.memoryCue: List = order; Dictionary = lookup; HashSet = unique; Queue = FIFO.

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and ICollection and IList?
questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable represents enumeration, ICollection adds collection-level operations such as Count and mutation-related members, and IList adds indexed access.
questions.example: A method returning IEnumerable<Transaction> communicates that callers only need to enumerate results.
questions.detailedAnswer: Returning the narrowest useful abstraction reduces coupling. IList implies ordering and indexing semantics that may not be needed.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose the interface based on the contract the caller needs, not the concrete collection I happen to use internally.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming IEnumerable always means a database query; assuming IList is always faster.

questions.question: What is the difference between const, readonly and static readonly?
questions.shortAnswer: const is a compile-time constant, readonly can be assigned during declaration or construction, and static readonly has one runtime value shared by the type.
questions.example: A fixed protocol value may be const, while a generated configuration or immutable service-level value may be static readonly.
questions.detailedAnswer: const values are embedded into consuming assemblies, so changing a public const can require consumers to recompile.
questions.seniorPerspective: I prefer readonly for values determined at runtime or constructed from configuration.
questions.commonMistakes: Using const for values that may change across deployments; assuming readonly means compile-time constant.

questions.question: What is the difference between ref, out and in parameters?
questions.shortAnswer: ref requires the caller to initialize the variable, out requires the method to assign it, and in passes a value by readonly reference.
questions.example: A parsing method may use out for a parsed result, while ref can update an existing value.
questions.detailedAnswer: These keywords affect calling semantics and can avoid copies for some value types, but they should be used only when the API benefits from them.
questions.seniorPerspective: For public APIs I prefer clear return types or result objects when multiple outputs are becoming hard to understand.
questions.commonMistakes: Thinking out must be initialized by the caller; using ref everywhere for performance without measurement.

questions.question: What is the difference between string and StringBuilder?
questions.shortAnswer: string is immutable, so repeated concatenation can create new strings. StringBuilder is designed for repeated modifications.
questions.example: Building a large ATM journal message in a loop is a case where StringBuilder can reduce intermediate allocations.
questions.detailedAnswer: For a few concatenations interpolation is usually clearer. StringBuilder is useful for substantial iterative construction.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on workload and readability, not because StringBuilder is always faster.
questions.commonMistakes: Using StringBuilder for every string; forgetting to measure small operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throw ex?
questions.shortAnswer: throw preserves the original stack trace, while throw ex resets the throw location and loses useful diagnostic context.
questions.example: In production RCA, preserving the original stack trace is critical for finding the real failing method.
questions.detailedAnswer: Wrap exceptions only when adding meaningful context, and preserve the original exception as the inner exception.
questions.seniorPerspective: I avoid catching an exception unless I can handle it, translate it, add context, or perform required cleanup.
questions.commonMistakes: Using throw ex; losing the original stack location; catching Exception everywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: checked enables overflow checking for integral arithmetic, while unchecked allows overflow to wrap according to the numeric type rules.
questions.example: A financial calculation converting amounts or counters should consider overflow behaviour explicitly.
questions.detailedAnswer: The right choice depends on whether overflow is an invalid condition that should fail or an expected low-level operation.
questions.seniorPerspective: For financial values I prefer decimal and explicit validation rather than relying on overflow behaviour.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming decimal overflow behaves exactly like int overflow; ignoring boundary validation.
followUps: What exception does checked overflow produce for integral arithmetic?
questions.memoryCue: checked = detect overflow; unchecked = allow it.

questions.question: What are extension methods in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Extension methods let you add callable methods to an existing type without modifying or inheriting from that type.
questions.example: A project can define ToAuditMessage(this Transaction transaction) as a reusable formatting helper.
questions.detailedAnswer: They are static methods with a this parameter on the first argument. They improve discoverability but can also hide dependencies if overused.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use them for cohesive reusable operations, not to turn every utility into a pseudo-instance API.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting business-critical stateful behaviour into extensions; creating ambiguous overloads.
followUps: Can extension methods override instance methods?

questions.question: What is a sealed class in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A sealed class cannot be inherited. A sealed override prevents further overriding of a virtual member.
questions.example: A security-sensitive component might be sealed when inheritance would violate its invariants.
questions.detailedAnswer: Sealing communicates that extension through inheritance is not part of the supported design.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use it when inheritance would be unsafe or the type's contract should remain closed.
questions.commonMistakes: Using sealed everywhere without understanding extensibility requirements.
followUps: Can a sealed class implement interfaces?

questions.question: What is an indexer in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: An indexer lets an object expose array-like access syntax for its internal representation.
questions.example: A configuration collection can expose settings by key using an indexer.
questions.detailedAnswer: Indexers are useful when the object conceptually represents a collection or lookup.
questions.seniorPerspective: I keep indexer behaviour predictable and validate missing keys explicitly.
questions.commonMistakes: Using indexers to hide expensive operations or network calls.
followUps: Can an indexer be overloaded?

questions.question: What are iterators and yield return in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: An iterator lets a method produce a sequence lazily using yield return. The caller requests items as it enumerates.
questions.example: A large transaction stream can be processed without creating a complete list in memory.
questions.detailedAnswer: Iterator execution is deferred until enumeration and state is maintained between yields.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use iterators when streaming or lazy generation is valuable, but I watch for repeated enumeration and resource lifetime issues.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming the iterator runs when the method is called; returning a sequence over disposed resources.
followUps: yield break vs yield return?
questions.memoryCue: yield = produce one item at a time.

questions.question: What are records in C# and when would you use them?
questions.shortAnswer: Records are designed for data-centric models with value-based equality and convenient immutable-style syntax.
questions.example: An API response or command DTO can be a record when identity is defined by its data.
questions.detailedAnswer: Records reduce boilerplate for equality and copying. They do not make every nested object deeply immutable.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use records for value-like messages and DTOs, while entities with identity and lifecycle are usually classes.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming records are always immutable; using records for entities without considering identity semantics.

questions.question: What is pattern matching in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Pattern matching lets code test type, value and shape conditions concisely using is, switch expressions and property patterns.
questions.example: An ATM transaction can be handled based on its runtime type and important properties.
questions.detailedAnswer: Pattern matching can make branching explicit and exhaustive, especially with switch expressions.
questions.seniorPerspective: I prefer it when the branching is genuinely based on shape/type; polymorphism may be better when behaviour belongs to the type itself.
questions.commonMistakes: Creating huge switch expressions that become a substitute for polymorphism.

questions.question: What is covariance and contravariance in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Covariance allows a more derived generic type to be used where a base type is expected for output positions; contravariance works in the opposite direction for input positions.
questions.example: IEnumerable<Derived> can be assigned to IEnumerable<Base> because IEnumerable<out T> is covariant.
questions.detailedAnswer: Variance applies to interfaces and delegates with compatible in/out positions and is useful for API flexibility.
questions.seniorPerspective: I check whether a generic parameter is consumed or produced before reasoning about variance.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming List<T> is covariant; forgetting that mutable collections cannot safely expose covariance.

questions.question: What is the difference between IDisposable and a finalizer?
questions.shortAnswer: IDisposable provides deterministic cleanup initiated by code, while a finalizer is a GC-driven fallback for unmanaged resources.
questions.example: A database connection or file handle should be disposed deterministically rather than waiting for GC.
questions.detailedAnswer: The using statement or declaration ensures Dispose is called even when exceptions occur. Finalizers are expensive and uncommon in application code.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use SafeHandle or existing disposable abstractions instead of writing finalizers unless directly managing unmanaged resources.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming GC immediately releases file handles; writing finalizers for every class.
followUps: What does using translate to?
questions.memoryCue: Dispose = deterministic cleanup; GC = memory management.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
questions.shortAnswer: The GC automatically reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable. It uses generations to optimise collection based on object lifetime.
questions.example: A high-throughput API may create many short-lived request objects, which are usually collected in younger generations.
questions.detailedAnswer: GC manages managed memory, not arbitrary external resources. Gen 0/1/2 and the Large Object Heap are important when diagnosing allocation pressure.
questions.seniorPerspective: For production issues I measure allocations and GC pauses rather than assuming GC is the cause.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying GC collects objects simply because a variable went out of scope; confusing unmanaged resources with managed memory.

questions.question: What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected application?
questions.shortAnswer: A memory leak occurs when objects remain reachable even though the application no longer needs them, so GC cannot reclaim them.
questions.example: A long-lived singleton subscribing to events from many short-lived objects can accidentally keep those objects alive.
questions.detailedAnswer: Common causes include static collections, event subscriptions, caches without eviction and closures retaining large graphs.
questions.seniorPerspective: I investigate memory leaks with heap snapshots, allocation profiling and object-reference paths rather than calling GC.Collect as a fix.
questions.commonMistakes: Thinking GC eliminates all leaks; forcing GC instead of finding the retaining reference.
followUps: How can events keep objects alive?
questions.memoryCue: Leak = still reachable but no longer needed.

questions.question: What is reflection in C# and when should you use it?
questions.shortAnswer: Reflection inspects metadata and types at runtime and can dynamically create or invoke members.
questions.example: A plugin framework can discover classes implementing IPlugin at startup.
questions.detailedAnswer: Reflection is powerful but can add complexity and runtime cost. Source generators or explicit registration may be better when the set of types is known.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use reflection at boundaries such as plugin discovery or framework infrastructure and keep hot paths strongly typed.

questions.question: What are attributes in C#?

questions.example: An API action can use an attribute to declare authorization or validation metadata.
questions.detailedAnswer: Attributes are declarative metadata; the framework decides what that metadata means.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use attributes for cross-cutting metadata and framework integration, while keeping core business rules explicit.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting complex business logic inside attributes.

questions.question: What is the difference between dynamic and var in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: var is statically typed at compile time; dynamic defers member binding to runtime.
questions.example: var is appropriate for ordinary strongly typed local variables, while dynamic may be used for interoperability with COM or genuinely dynamic data.
questions.detailedAnswer: dynamic can move errors from compile time to runtime and can affect tooling and performance.

questions.question: What is the difference between a constructor and a static constructor?
questions.shortAnswer: An instance constructor initializes each object, while a static constructor initializes type-level state once before the type is first used.
questions.example: A transaction object can validate its instance dependencies in its constructor, while a static configuration cache may use a static constructor.
questions.detailedAnswer: Static constructors cannot be called directly and have no parameters.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why does it support OOP design?
questions.shortAnswer: Dependency injection supplies a class's collaborators from outside instead of making the class construct them itself.
questions.example: A TransactionService can receive IAuditLogger and IPaymentGateway through its constructor.
questions.detailedAnswer: DI supports dependency inversion and makes substitution and testing easier.

questions.question: What is operator overloading in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Operator overloading lets a user-defined type define meaningful behaviour for operators such as +, -, == or >.
questions.example: A Money value object can define addition while preserving currency rules.
questions.detailedAnswer: Overloaded operators should be intuitive and consistent with equality and domain semantics.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use them for value objects where the operator meaning is obvious, not to make domain operations cryptic.

questions.question: How do Equals, == and GetHashCode relate in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: Equals defines logical equality, == may be overloaded, and GetHashCode must return the same hash for equal objects.
questions.example: A transaction value object should compare based on its identity fields and behave consistently in dictionaries and hash sets.
questions.detailedAnswer: If equality semantics change, GetHashCode must remain consistent with them.
